entities.summary:
Józef Zabiełło h. Topór (died May 9, 1794), a prominent Polish-Lithuanian nobleman of the szlachta, emerged as a controversial figure during the terminal decline of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in the late 18th century. His career, marked by a rapid ascent through state offices from Grand Master of the Hunt in 1775 to Field Hetman of Lithuania in 1793, inextricably linked him with the forces that ultimately dismantled the Commonwealth. Zabiełło's unwavering alignment with the Russian Empire, particularly during the critical period of the Great Sejm (1788–1792) and the subsequent partitions, rendered him a symbol of the internal divisions and external pressures that led to the nation's collapse.

Zabiełło's political trajectory saw him appointed as konsyliarz of the Permanent Council in 1782, a body often perceived as an instrument of Russian influence. He served as a deputy from Samogitia to the Great Sejm, where he became a vocal opponent of the Constitution of May 3, 1791, and a staunch supporter of the Targowica Confederation. This confederation, formed in 1792 with Russian backing, aimed to overturn the reforms of the Constitution and restore the old 'Golden Liberty,' effectively inviting Russian military intervention. His elevation to Field Hetman of Lithuania in 1793, following the Second Partition of Poland and under direct Russian pressure, cemented his role as a collaborator with foreign powers.

entities.summary:
Józef Zabiełło h. Topór (died 1794), a Polish-Lithuanian nobleman (szlachcic), rose to prominence in the late 18th-century Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth as a figure emblematic of the deep internal divisions and foreign manipulation that ultimately led to the state's demise. Serving as Lithuanian Grand Master of the Hunt from 1775, a konsyliarz of the Permanent Council from 1782, and later as a deputy from Samogitia to the Great Sejm (1788–1792), Zabiełło consistently championed pro-Russian policies, aligning himself with the powerful forces seeking to undermine the Commonwealth's sovereignty. His career path reflects the profound political and moral compromises made by some elites during a period of intense geopolitical pressure. 

His most consequential actions occurred in the final years of the Commonwealth. As a staunch opponent of the May 3rd Constitution, Zabiełło became a leading member of the Targowica Confederation in 1792, an alliance of magnates and nobles who invited Russian intervention to overthrow the reformist government. Following the successful Russian-backed intervention and the subsequent Second Partition of Poland in 1793, Zabiełło was rewarded with the coveted and strategically important position of Field Hetman of Lithuania. In this role, he effectively dismantled the Lithuanian army, facilitating Russian control and further weakening the Commonwealth's capacity for self-defense against partitioning powers. His command was characterized by corruption and a blatant disregard for national interests, contributing directly to the state's military impotence.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Józef Zabiełło's actions as a pro-Russian magnate and Field Hetman directly contributed to the military and political weakening of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, leading to its Second Partition. His public execution became a potent symbol of national resistance against betrayal during the Kościuszko Uprising.
